issue_context.title: Nested hit objects are leaked when parent hit object is edited or deleted
issue_context.body:
1. Inspect `Playfield.lifetimeEntryMap.Count` while editing a slider shape.
2. See the number is increasing rapidly.

Nested hit objects should be removed when the parent hit object is removed or when the nested hit objects are recreated by `ApplyDefaults`.

It is a visual issue for osu!catch editor because new nested hit objects will be stacked every frame while the parent object is edited, resulting in a massive amount of stacked objects.
comments:
Came across this one again while investigating #20208.

![Parallels Desktop 2022-09-12 at 08 44 26](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/191335/189610945-fd7e4496-f931-4dfc-9d17-c92cc8a206cf.png)

review_comments: How is this safe? `OnDefaultsApplied` looks to be called after the new nested hitobjects have been created, not before. So if it's clearing `childEntries`, isn't it going to be removing entries of the new nested hitobjects?

Just so I understand correctly, this seems to only be safe because the order of operations is:
- Hitobject changes.
- `HitObject.ApplyDefaults()`
- `HitObject.DefaultsApplied`
- `HitObjectEntryManager.onDefaultsApplied()`  (clears list)
- `DrawableHitObject.onDefaultsApplied()`
- `DrawableHitObject.Apply()`
- `Playfield.GetPooledDrawableRepresentation()` (for each nested object)
- `HitObjectEntryManager.Add()` (adds to list)

If I'm reading things correctly? I still find this pretty dodge and hard to follow, but I don't have any suggestions.

I also don't understand the purpose of this line in general. As far as I understand it, this is what this method does:
- `childrenMap[hitObject] -> childEntries`
- `childEntries.Clear()`
- `childrenMap[hitObject] <- childEntries`
It looks like this operation, the last one in my list above, is a no-op? Am I missing something?
I understand now why this is done the way it is, everything relies on that `.Remove()` call. I'm going to refactor this because it's hard to understand and easy to miss.

Well, I didn't end up changing this. The idea I had was to not do the whole `.Remove()` stuff altogether, but in hindsight this is probably the more performance way of doing things anyway.

I added what I believe is appropriate commenting along the way, tho.
